Wall Street loses only 0.4% despite Jensen Huang's departure: AMD and Broadcom jump nearly 6%, the US 10-year yield climbs back above 5%

On Thursday, November 12, Nvidia plunged as much as 14% after its chief executive resigned, then closed down just 4.34%. The main US indexes fell about 0.4%, held back mostly by higher oil prices and interest rates, while Nvidia's rivals soared. On Friday, Tokyo kept rising [1][2][3][5][10].

The Dow Jones closed at 52,297.09 points (-0.36%), the S&P 500 at 7,592.40 (-0.35%) and the Nasdaq at 25,366.09 (-0.39%), after falling as much as 1.6% during the session [1][2]. The Russell 2000 of small companies fell 1.7% [4].
Nvidia fell as much as 14%, then only 4.34% at the close [2][3]. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim replacement for Jensen Huang [3].
AMD gained 5.9% and Broadcom 5.5%: investors are betting that these rivals will take a bigger share of the AI chip market [1][2][8].
The real drag came from bonds, which reopened after the November 11 holiday: the yield on 10-year US government debt jumped by more than 0.13 points to 5.125%, and the 2-year yield to 4.879% [5].
Markets now see a Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hike in December as certain [5]. Beth Hammack, president of the Cleveland Fed, believes rates still need to rise, in smaller steps [6].

Brent closed at $95.82 a barrel (+3.3%), and US crude at $88.74 (+2.6%), after explosions on four tankers in Hormuz announced by the Iranian army and Houthi attacks on Saudi sites [7]. Donald Trump said: “We don't need a deal with Iran” [7][12].
The European Stoxx 600 closed at a record 664.01 points [9]. On Friday, Tokyo's Nikkei was up about 1.25%, on track for its best week since June (+7.3%), with Advantest up 5.9% [10].

Key takeaway: the abrupt exit of the boss of the biggest chip company did not cause a crash. Money moved from Nvidia to its rivals, and it was rather oil and rising rates that pushed Wall Street down [1][5][7][8].
A 10-year yield above 5% weighs on stocks: when a risk-free investment pays more than 5% a year, riskier shares become less attractive, and borrowing costs companies and households more [5].
Oil links the war with Iran to the markets: a pricier barrel fuels inflation, which pushes the Fed to raise its rates. Over the week, however, it was still down about 2.5% [7].
Next week will be busy for AI stocks: Anthropic plans to set the price of its stock market debut on November 18, for a first listing on the 19th, under the symbol “ANT” [11].

For you, the concrete effect comes through rates and oil: US rates pull European ones up (the French 10-year yield rose to 4.85% on Thursday), and so the cost of loans, and a pricier barrel shows up at the pump [7][13]. No buy or sell advice here.

Spain: the campaign for the November 29 snap general election is under way, with the right in the lead but dependent on Vox

At midnight on the night of November 12-13, the campaign for the snap general election of November 29 opened in Spain with the traditional poster pasting. Polls give the edge to the People's Party (right), which would need the far-right Vox to govern, against Pedro Sánchez's Socialists [1][2][3].

The official campaign started at 12:00 a.m. on November 13 and will run until midnight on Friday the 27th, followed by a day of reflection. Spaniards will elect the 350 members of parliament and the senators [2][3].
According to Reuters, Alberto Núñez Feijóo's People's Party (PP) would beat the Socialists (PSOE) but would need Vox to get a majority, which is 176 seats out of 350 [1].

A 40dB poll for El País sees the PP-PSOE gap narrowing to 2 points, with about 190 seats for the right-wing bloc; a SocioMétrica poll for El Español gives the PP and Vox around 200 seats together [1].

Pollsters diverge: SW Demoscopia (November 7) puts the PSOE ahead, at 30.8% against 28.8% for the PP, 17.2% for Vox and 7.7% for Sumar; the CIS, the public pollster, gave the PSOE 34% and the PP 22.2% in October [4].
To the left of the PSOE, parties failed to agree on a joint list, which lowers Sánchez's chances of forming a coalition; Podemos risks losing its seats [1].
Housing, immigration and corruption are expected to dominate the campaign, along with the aftermath of the deadly train accident that led Transport Minister Óscar Puente to resign [1][6].

The campaign opens two days after the first general strike in 14 years, on November 11: 120,000 demonstrators in Madrid according to the prefecture, more than half a million according to the Tenants' Union, more than 50,000 in Barcelona, and more than 70 arrests [5].
Key takeaway: Spain could swing to the right, with the far-right Vox in the position of kingmaker to form a majority [1].
These snap elections are taking place in a tense social climate: housing crisis, wages seen as too low, and anger after the rail disaster [1][5].
The gaps between polls are unusually large, from 2 points to more than 10 depending on the pollster, which makes the outcome more uncertain than it looks [1][4].
The division of the radical left, which is running without a joint list, may cost seats to Sánchez's camp and complicate any left-wing coalition [1].

For you, Spain is a neighbor and a major destination for the French. A change of majority could alter its policy on housing, immigration and Europe, and weigh on the balance within the European Council, where rules that also apply in France are decided.

China: state-owned giant Huafa, with 545 billion yuan of debt, loses its “AAA” rating and unsettles the bond market

Huafa, a conglomerate owned by the city of Zhuhai in southern China, saw the agency Fitch downgrade its rating by two notches. The group then cut ties with the Chinese agency that gave it the best possible rating, “AAA”. Investors are wondering how far Chinese cities can support their indebted companies [1][3][4].

The US rating agency Fitch lowered Zhuhai Huafa Group's rating from BBB to BB+, two notches at once, and downgraded its bonds in the same way [1][3]. The rating remains on “negative watch”: a further cut is possible [1].
Fitch's stated reason: it now judges both the city of Zhuhai's ability to support Huafa and the likelihood that it will do so to be weaker [1][3].

Huafa then ended its contract with the Chinese agency China Lianhe Credit Rating. The agency withdrew the group's rating and those of 16 of its bonds, all of which were rated “AAA” [1][4]. On November 4, Lianhe had still maintained this “AAA”, while placing it on negative watch [4].
The weight of the debt: 544.794 billion yuan of liabilities as of September 30, 2026, and debt of more than 75% relative to what the group owns [4].

Huafa's bonds had already fallen about two weeks before Fitch's decision. A broker cited by the South China Morning Post says his bank has barred its staff from opening new positions on these securities. The selling wave even hit government bonds [1].

Huafa insists it is meeting its obligations: the group paid two coupons (the interest owed to lenders) on time, and Zhuhai's public capital says it is backing repayments [5]. At the same time, the city's state-owned companies are reorganizing their assets: the Gree group is to take over Huafa's Marriott hotel for about 2 billion yuan [6].

Key takeaway: in China, many investors lend to city-owned companies believing that the state will always pay. Fitch is saying plainly that this support is no longer guaranteed for Huafa, which raises doubts about a whole category of debt [1][3].

A rating is an opinion on the risk that a borrower will not repay. Going from BBB to BB+ means leaving the so-called “investment” category for the “speculative” one: many funds are no longer allowed to buy these securities, and the group has to pay more to borrow.

It all began in late October: on the 29th, Fitch had placed Huafa on watch, citing revenues that cover debt service less and less, large short-term maturities and widening spreads, that is, a growing extra cost of borrowing [2].
By leaving Lianhe rather than accepting a cut to its “AAA”, Huafa avoids a bad Chinese rating, but the market sees it as one more warning sign [1][4].

For you, the direct impact is small: few European savers hold these bonds. But the debt of companies tied to Chinese cities is a weak point of the Chinese economy; if it seizes up, Chinese growth and its purchases in Europe suffer.

Canada: the only non-European country at the Dublin summit, Carney pushes his “associate member” plan for the EU before heading off to Asia

On Thursday, November 12, in Dublin, Mark Carney was the only non-European leader at the European Political Community summit. The Canadian Prime Minister defended his plan to make Canada the first “associate member” of the European Union, the first stop of a tour that then takes him to Asia to sign trade agreements [1][2][4].

The European Political Community is an informal gathering of leaders from across the continent, held every six months since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 [3]. For the second time, Canada was the only non-European country at the table [1].
Canada and the EU are working to make Canada the Union's “first associate member”, according to the Prime Minister's office [1]. This status does not yet have a precise definition [3].

This plan extends the “Alliance for the Future”, launched last month at the Canada-EU summit in Montreal with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the Commission, and António Costa, president of the European Council [1].

Carney met the Greek and Cypriot leaders: their countries have not yet ratified CETA, the free trade agreement between Canada and the EU, largely applied since 2017 [2]. France and Ireland have not ratified it either [2]. Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides pledged to get it ratified [2].

On Ukraine, Carney heard Volodymyr Zelensky on the negotiations with Russia [2]. He summed up: “Security guarantees are a European responsibility, with Canada, with the United States. So there are several layers” [2].
He also spoke on the sidelines with Emmanuel Macron and the leaders of Latvia, Ireland and Denmark [2].

The tour, from November 11 to 19, then goes through the Philippines, Cambodia and China [4]. In Manila, at the ASEAN (Southeast Asia) summit, Ottawa wants to finalize a free trade agreement opening up more than $3.5 billion in exports, and to conclude an agreement with the Philippines meant to triple trade by 2035 [4].

Key takeaway: facing US tariffs, Canada is looking for other customers and other allies, first in Europe, then in Asia. Carney presents these ties as a way to lower the cost of living for Canadians [2][4].

With Washington, talks mainly concern so-called “Section 232” tariffs (justified by national security): up to 50% on Canadian steel and 25% on cars [6]. The minister in charge of relations with the United States, Dominic LeBlanc, believes Trump's strategy has not changed after the Democrats' victory in the midterm elections [7].
CETA is not yet fully in force until all EU countries have ratified it: this is why Carney is courting Athens and Nicosia [2].
The tour ends in Shenzhen, China, at the APEC summit, the Asia-Pacific economic forum [4].

For you, this rapprochement can matter: a Canada more closely tied to the EU means more trade with a major producer of oil, gas, minerals and grain. On the French side, CETA remains a sensitive subject, notably for livestock farmers, and France still has not ratified it.

Colombia-Venezuela: after two kidnappings blamed on the ELN guerrillas, Caracas promises to cooperate to secure the border

On Thursday, November 12, Colombia and Venezuela said they were ready to coordinate their fight against crime at their border, after two kidnappings: that of a mayor's wife on Wednesday, and that of an army officer on November 4. Bogotá is also asking for US help [1][3][4].

Nancy Gómez, wife of Jaime Luis Buitrago, mayor of Uribia (La Guajira region, northeast), was abducted on Wednesday, November 11, around 6:10 a.m. by armed men near a gym, then taken away in a white van [3]. Authorities believe she was taken to Venezuela [1].
Authorities provisionally attribute the kidnapping to the National Liberation Army (ELN) [5]. Other armed groups are present in the area, including FARC dissidents [3].
President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered the full deployment of the security forces and a “plan cadenas”, which consists of blocking roads to stop the kidnappers from crossing into Venezuela [2].
On November 4, Second Lieutenant María Camila Pantoja was kidnapped in Saravena, in Arauca department; the ELN claimed responsibility for the abduction [4][1].
Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora asked Washington to help secure Venezuela's intelligence cooperation to locate her [4][1]. Her whereabouts are unknown [1].
Caracas says it is “fully willing to carry out all necessary coordination” with Colombian authorities [1]. The two countries share 2,219 kilometers of border [1].

Key takeaway: Colombia has long accused Venezuela of harboring ELN and FARC guerrillas, which Caracas has always denied [1]. This promise of cooperation is therefore a change of tone, tied to the ongoing political transition in Venezuela [1][7].

Jorge Eduardo Mora says he hopes this transition will bring real cooperation [1]. In Venezuela, Delcy Rodríguez is serving as interim president and promises elections, which opposition leader María Corina Machado would like to see sooner [8].

Washington weighs on this game: the United States is pushing Caracas to follow a phased transition plan, and Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco met Secretary of State Marco Rubio on November 2 [7].
The ELN shows it remains able to strike very visible targets, a mayor's wife and an officer, which puts border security front and center for President De la Espriella [2][4][5].

For you, the direct impact is small. But the stability of this border matters for migration, drug trafficking to Europe and the revival of Venezuelan oil, which Western companies are watching closely.

COP31: Australia, which leads the negotiations, champions the Pacific but is criticized over its coal and gas

At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese centered his speech on the Pacific islands and their climate fund, which has reached $200 million. Criticized for not mentioning fossil fuels, he defends himself. His minister Chris Bowen, who leads the negotiations, begins the final stretch [1][2][5].

COP31 is being held from November 9 to 20, 2026 in Antalya [7]. Turkey presides over it, but Australia leads the negotiations: its Climate Minister Chris Bowen has to get more than 190 countries to agree [2][5].

In his speech to leaders, Anthony Albanese put the Pacific at the center, as his island neighbors need urgent action from the world [1]. He defended not having mentioned fossil fuels: he wanted to focus attention on the Pacific's needs [1].

He called for support for the Pacific Resilience Facility, a fund launched in 2025 to raise US$500 million for climate adaptation. He presented it as the “promise to our Pacific family that it will not face the climate crisis alone” [5].

The fund passed the US$200 million mark at COP31, helped by its first philanthropic donation: US$5 million from billionaire Andrew Forrest's Minderoo Foundation [5]. Australia has committed US$100 million to it [1].

Before the speech, more than 500 academics signed an open letter: in their view, Australia cannot lead the climate fight while expanding coal and gas at home [1]. Amnesty International Australia says the same [8].

Chris Bowen told Reuters: “My job is to guide consensus, not to bang the table demanding specific action” [3][4]. In his view, the idea that Australian exports undermine his role “does not stand up to the reality of a COP negotiation” [5].

Key takeaway: Australia is steering the COP31 negotiations while continuing to expand its coal and gas production. This balancing act is at the heart of the criticism, one week before the end of the summit [1][2].

The challenge is immense: over two days of speeches, leaders set out opposing demands. Small islands want immediate emissions cuts, Europeans bet on electrification, developing countries demand money [4]. Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, asserted her country's “sovereign right” to develop its oil [4].
On November 11, UN Secretary-General António Guterres declared that keeping the 1.5°C goal “means no new coal” [6].

Chris Bowen promises a “pragmatic” approach that takes into account countries' very different levels of renewable energy [2]. He points out that the call to “transition away from fossil fuels”, adopted at COP28 in Dubai, was an Australian suggestion [9].

For you, this COP decides the pace of the exit from fossil fuels and the money paid to vulnerable countries, to which Europe contributes. A weak deal pushes efforts back, a strong deal speeds up the transition here too.

Brazil: Banco do Brasil halves its profit forecast, dragged down by farmers who no longer repay, and falls 8% on the stock market

On Thursday, November 12, the major Brazilian state-owned bank reported a quarterly profit down 66.5% and cut its 2026 forecast to 9 to 11 billion reais, from 18 to 22 billion. Its shares fell 8.35%, its worst reaction to results in 18 months [1][2].
In the third quarter, adjusted profit falls to 1.27 billion reais, 66.5% less than a year earlier, and below analysts' expectations [1][2].
For 2026, the bank now targets an adjusted profit of 9 to 11 billion reais, instead of the 18 to 22 billion announced in May: the forecast is roughly cut in half [1].
The cost of risk (the money set aside for loans that will not be repaid) reaches 21.2 billion reais for the quarter [3]. New loans in default amount to 28 billion reais across the whole bank [4].
The share of profit paid out to shareholders is cut to the legal minimum of 25%, a measure presented as temporary to protect capital [3].

Chair Tarciana Medeiros accuses some “medium and large rural producers” of having stopped paying without offering guarantees to renegotiate [2]. She speaks of deliberate moral hazard, since some are not repaying despite record harvests [4].

The share closed at 15.48 reais (-8.35%), about 8 billion reais of market value lost [2]. The Ibovespa index fell 0.43% to 171,324 points, and the real lost about 1%, to 5.64 per dollar, its lowest closing level in 12 months [5].

Key takeaway: the state-controlled bank, Brazilian farmers' top lender, is paying for the defaults of part of the farming world. Its profitability is collapsing and its shareholders, including the state, will receive lower dividends [1][3].
The shock comes at a bad time: Brazilian banks had already plunged after Lula's reelection on October 26, and investors worry about public finances and higher interest rates for longer [5][8].
It is also a signal about agriculture, the engine of Brazil's exports: if farmers stop repaying banks, credit for the next harvest will become scarcer and more expensive [3][4].

For you, the direct impact is small: Banco do Brasil has little weight in mainstream European funds. But Brazil is a giant in soy, coffee and meat: an agricultural credit crisis there could eventually weigh on global supply and prices. No buy or sell advice here.

How it works: why defaults crush a bank's profit

A bank makes money on the gap between the interest it receives on its loans and what it pays on the money it borrows. But when customers stop repaying, it has to set aside a reserve, called a provision, to cover the expected loss [3]. These provisions are deducted directly from profit. At Banco do Brasil, they reached 21.2 billion reais in a single quarter, which explains a profit that fell to 1.27 billion [2][3]. To keep enough capital, the safety cushion required by the authorities, the bank also pays out less in dividends: only the legal minimum of 25% of profit [3].
